title: Making event delivery predictable
summary: A synthetic backend case study about retrying safely, handling duplicates, and making failure visible.
highlights: A recovery path operators can inspect
problem: In this fictional scenario, an integration sends the same event more than once and downstream services occasionally time out. A successful retry must not repeat the business action.
The example explores a small, understandable design rather than an exactly-once guarantee.
constraints: Assume at-least-once delivery and temporary downstream failures.
Keep the operational state visible without exposing customer payloads.
contribution: This is a synthetic example, not a claim of personal work. An engineer in this scenario would define delivery states, a deduplication boundary, and a recovery workflow.
Team-level deployment, security review, and production operation are not claimed.

decisions.title: Make retries safe before making them automatic
decisions.choice: Record a stable event key and the resulting state in the same transaction as the local business change.
decisions.alternative: Retry every timeout and assume the first attempt failed.
decisions.tradeoff: The transaction adds storage and cleanup work, but avoids treating an ambiguous network response as proof that nothing happened.

decisions.title: Stop retrying when a person needs to decide
decisions.choice: Use bounded backoff and a failed-delivery queue with an explicit replay action.
decisions.alternative: Retry indefinitely without exposing an operator workflow.
decisions.tradeoff: A recovery queue needs ownership and clear diagnostics. It makes unresolved failures visible instead of hiding them in an endless loop.

results.claim: The design illustrates how one event can be retried without repeating a local side effect.
results.basis: Synthetic reasoning only. No production system, benchmark, or measured improvement is represented.

limitations: Cross-service atomicity is not guaranteed. A downstream system still needs an explicit idempotency contract.
lessons: Name ambiguous states instead of pretending every request is a clear success or failure.
nextSteps: For a real project, verify the failure model with duplicate, timeout, replay, and partial-completion tests.

diagram.title: A public-safe delivery model
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  event[Incoming event] --> worker[Delivery worker]
  worker --> store[(State and deduplication)]
  worker --> consumer[Idempotent consumer]
  worker --> recovery[Recovery queue]

  classDef process fill:#ccfbf1,stroke:#0f766e,color:#134e4a

  class worker,consumer process
  class store data
  class recovery recovery
diagram.description: An incoming event reaches a worker. The worker records delivery state and deduplication data, calls an idempotent consumer, and sends unresolved failures to a recovery queue.
